summary_plain: Moves about 56 arcseconds per hour across 4 images over 14.7 hours. Only two sightings, so the motion is unconfirmed.

known_object.observer: SPHEREx (geocentric JPL predictions corrected with the spacecraft position from the FITS headers)

scores.definition: Rule-based ranking score in [0, 1]: motion_consistency x snr x (1 - artifact_likelihood). It orders candidates for review. It is not a probability.

vetting.description: Number of separate visits (clusters of exposures hours apart) the object was seen in
Lowest signal-to-noise ratio among the detections
Scatter of the detections about the fitted motion, arcsec
Chi-square probability of the motion fit given the position errors (informational)
Fraction of detections whose aperture touches pixels SPHEREx flags as unreliable (phantom, dichroic, nonlinear, persistence)
Median fraction of the aperture flux in the brightest pixel (a cosmic ray or hot pixel puts nearly all of it in one pixel)
Smallest distance of a detection from the edge of the image data, pixels
Highest combined forced-photometry S/N at the object's first position in any other visit (a static star would be detected there)
Ratio of the 90th to 10th percentile detection flux across the wavelengths sampled
Matched to a known asteroid or comet by JPL (filled in at request time)

error_sources.label: Cosmic-ray hit or one-off glitch
error_sources.explanation: A particle strike or electronic glitch can make a dot appear in a single image.
error_sources.evidence: Seen in 4 exposures during 2 separate visits.

error_sources.label: Bad pixels, ghosts or detector defects
error_sources.explanation: Hot pixels, optical ghosts or pixels flagged by the SPHEREx pipeline can mimic a source.

error_sources.label: Unrelated dots linked together
error_sources.explanation: Separate faint dots in different images can line up by chance.
error_sources.evidence: Only two sightings: any two dots define a straight line.

error_sources.label: A star or galaxy that didn't move
error_sources.explanation: A fixed source near the detection limit can come and go between images.
error_sources.evidence: Nothing at the first position in other visits (combined S/N at most 3.5).

error_sources.label: Brightness change caused by the filter, not the object
error_sources.explanation: SPHEREx sees each spot at a different infrared wavelength in each image, so brightness naturally changes from frame to frame.
error_sources.evidence: Detections span 1.45 to 1.73 µm; fluxes vary by a factor of 2.0.

error_sources.label: A catalogued asteroid or comet
error_sources.explanation: Most moving dots in SPHEREx images are asteroids that are already known.
error_sources.evidence: No match in JPL SBIdent and JPL Horizons within 15 arcsec.

error_sources.label: A real object missing from the catalogs we checked
error_sources.explanation: Some real asteroids are faint or newly found and are not in JPL's database yet.
error_sources.evidence: Cannot be ruled out from SPHEREx data alone.

explanation.text: Detected in 4 SPHEREx exposures spanning 14.7 hours. It moves 56.4 arcseconds per hour toward position angle 195 degrees. A straight-line fit leaves 1.86 arcseconds of scatter. Its faintest detection has a signal-to-noise ratio of 5.9. No catalogued asteroid or comet in JPL SBIdent and JPL Horizons was predicted within 15 arcseconds at every epoch. The closest catalogued object, 392574 (2011 SZ124), was 403.7 arcseconds away. Two sightings are not enough to confirm motion, so treat this as unconfirmed.

disclaimer: An unmatched candidate may be an imaging artifact, a measurement error, or an object missing from the catalogs we checked. This is not a discovery claim.
